trace.topic: SaaStr’s YouTube Crosses 5,000,000 Views. Our Top Videos and Sessions of All Time!
trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: The answer should connect audience growth to consistency, compounding content, or knowing what the audience repeatedly wants.
It should not just celebrate the milestone; it should explain the operating lesson behind it.
It should make content/community growth relevant to B2B founders.
rubric_must_haves: Turns the milestone into a founder lesson.
Includes at least one example of compounding distribution or content repetition.
Avoids sounding like a vanity-metrics post.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer says the real lesson behind five million views is not virality but compounding consistency. Founders learn what their audience values, keep shipping, and let repeated useful content build trust and distribution over time. The piece should make the case that community and media scale the same way product and GTM do: through repetition, iteration, and audience fit.
trace.prompt:
Write a blog post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: SaaStr’s YouTube Crosses 5,000,000 Views. Our Top Videos and Sessions of All Time!

Style examples from train-owned source text.
Use them for voice only. They are not evidence for claims.
Do not copy long passages verbatim.
[Style 1]
Dear SaaStr: How Can You Ensure a Smooth Transition When A New Team Member Takes Over a Customer Account?
Add value in the first interaction.  This is so rare.
There’s nothing more frustrating than getting a random email, “Hi, Tony is gone from the company. I know nothing about you, but I’m your new rep. Can we schedule a call?”
Find some way to add value.
One great way is to demo upcoming features / an upcoming release.
“Hi, I’m Jason, your next account exec. I’d love to find a way to help even more. Can I show you or anyone on your team the new AI features we’re launching shortly? There’s no additional cost for them and based on what I can see, they may radically increase your efficiency.”
Not perfect. But much better.
A second, albeit riskier, way to add value is to set up a call asking for “honest feedback on how we’re doing.”
This works, too.  Customers often just want to be heard.  The “problem” is you might have to do something about it.
[Style 2]
Dear SaaStr: When Is It Too Soon to Target Enterprise Customers in SaaS?
It too soon to target enterprise clients when you can’t support their needs 90 days
after
you close them.
It’s sort of OK in the enterprise to promise features and functionality that are sort of there … so long as you deliver them fairly promptly after the deal closes.
In fact, it happens all the time. Enterprise customers will even sign contracts agreeing to buy so long as you implement a key feature with X number of days.
But if you don’t have the team, commitment and experience to deliver that functionality at least X days after you close a Big Customer … you aren’t ready.  They’ll churn or at least, never fully deploy.
You don’t have to have the full enterprise package in the early days to close enterprise customers, especially if they have interest in you.  You’ll get some slack as a new, emerging vendor.  Especially if you have a strong deployment team.
But you have to meet your commitments and promises to them fairly soon after the deal closes.
More here:

So the
SaaStr YouTube channel is now crossing 500,000 subscribers!
And our #1 video — which also happened to be my very first ever video back in the day — has over 280,000 views!!
The first SaaStr video was one of the first SaaS sessions at Dreamforce way back in 2013!!  I remember walking down Market St to Moscone Center before the event, knowing this could change things 🙂
What were folks watching then?  A deep dive on “How To Build a SaaS Business”.
Fast forward to today, and we’ve done tons of great content since, including a deep dive on how to build a rocketship sales org, and how best to scale your marketing spend.
My personal favorite top 10 videos right below!

retrieval_hits.text:
So we’ve finally crossed 50,000 subs on SaaStr YouTube.  It took a while, but I’m probably on the unparalled quality of our content, especially the past 18+ months or so where we stepped up the editing and more.
So if you want to catch up, here are The Top 10 Most Popular SaaStr YouTube Sessions of All Time.  Note I did take out a few that would have made the list but were a bit dated etc:
#1,  279,000 Views: “How To Perfectly Pitch Your Seed Stage Startup With Y Combinator’s Michael Seibel:
Ycombinator is pretty popular
#2.  112,000 Views: “What’s New at WordPress with Matt Mullenweg, CEO of Automattic and Co-Founder of WordPress”
#3, 79,000 Views: “A Step by Step Guide to Revenue Growth with Mark Roberge, Harvard Business School”
#4.  62,526 Views: “From 2 Weeks of Runway to $1B Acquisition: The Founder Playbook with Loom’s CEO and Co-Founder”
#5.  46,771 Views: “From Burn-Out to $100M in ARR with Jason Cohen, Founder of WP Engine”
#6.  41,000 Views:  “Veeva: The Biggest Vertical SaaS Success Story of All Time” with Founder/CEO Peter Gassner
#7,  37,000 Views: “Sales Mistakes that Can Kill Your SaaS Business & How to Avoid Them”
#8.  36,000 Views:  “Twilio: The Inside Story with Jeff Lawson, CEO/Co-Founder”
#9.  35,266 Views: “The Secrets to YC’s Essential Startup Advice with Y Combinator with Michael Seibel”
#10.  33,270 Views: “How To Innovate Faster with Community: Insights From GitLab CEO Sid Sijbrandij”
